t: Maximum Good People Based on Statements — Bitmask Enumeration of Assignments
o: Good people always tell the truth; bad people are unconstrained, so an assignment of roles is valid exactly when every assumed-good person's statements agree with it. Example 1 resolves to 2 good people: persons 0 and 1 vouch for each other, and bad person 2's accusation is simply ignored. Example 2's mutual accusations cap the count at 1. Since n ≤ 15, all 2¹⁵ ≈ 32k assignments can be tested exhaustively: for a bitmask where bit i means person i is good, validity requires statements[i][j] = 1 ⇒ j good and statements[i][j] = 0 ⇒ j bad for every j, while statements made by bad people impose nothing at all.
k: Only statements made by assumed-good people constrain an assignment; bad people may say anything.
Validity check per mask: for each good i and each j, a 1 statement forces j ∈ mask and a 0 statement forces j ∉ mask.
The answer is the maximum popcount over valid masks — about 7.4M statement checks at n = 15.

a.i: Iterate masks from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1 treating bit i as person i being good. Verify every good person's statements against the mask and keep the largest valid popcount. The diagonal (statements[i][i] = 2) is naturally skipped by ignoring 2 entries.
s: For each mask in [0, 2ⁿ), assume bits encode goodness.
For every i set in the mask, scan statements[i][j]: reject if s == 1 and j is unset, or s == 0 and j is set.
If consistent, update the answer with popcount(mask).
a.t: O(2ⁿ · n²) — up to 32768 masks × ~225 statement checks each at n = 15.

a.n: Approach 2: Backtracking With Incremental Consistency Pruning
a.i: Assign people 0..n − 1 sequentially. When placing person pos, check consistency only against already-decided people: statements made by decided-good people about pos, and — if pos is assumed good — pos's own statements about them. Any contradiction prunes the whole subtree immediately, so in practice far fewer than 2ⁿ nodes get explored.
s: Recurse dfs(pos, cnt) carrying a good[] array of decisions so far.
To assign pos as bad: no decided-good k may have statements[k][pos] == 1; otherwise prune.
To assign pos as good: no decided-good k may have statements[k][pos] == 0, and every non-2 entry statements[pos][j] for decided j must match good[j].
At pos == n record cnt into the answer and backtrack.
a.t: Exponential, bounded by O(2ⁿ · n²) worst case — incremental checks cost O(n) per node and pruning usually cuts far more.
a.sp: O(n) — recursion depth plus the good array.

w: Say the validity criterion crisply before coding — bad people are witnesses without credibility, so only their goodness assumptions matter, never their statements. Enumeration is the safe interview answer given n ≤ 15; offer backtracking as the optimization discussion. Pitfalls: accidentally enforcing statements made by bad people (the most common bug), and forgetting that statements[i][i] = 2 must be skipped rather than validated. Follow-ups: return an actual witness assignment, maximize a weighted score of good people, or scale to larger n via constraint propagation.
